artifacts.notes:
WHAT THIS IS: uncorrected optical character recognition of a hand missal with two identified lettered-insert ranges mechanically excluded, 197,573 LF-terminated lines, landed as a plain source artifact and nothing more. It is deliberately NOT structured as liturgical records. The prior lt-hist corpus divided the same text into eleven markdown 'sections' whose only structural claim was a line range over the downloaded file, so a comparison of two such sections compares the scanner's disagreements rather than the liturgy's; nothing of that shape is reproduced here. Addressability by identity -- this collect, of this Mass -- belongs to passage records with real loci bound to physical line ranges over these exact bytes, which this schema already supports and which requires reading the pages rather than slicing the file. Until such a passage exists, this artifact is a finding aid.

WHAT SURVIVED THE INSERT EXCLUSIONS, STATED SO IT IS NOT DISCOVERED LATER. The excised pages are gone, but references to them remain in the body because they are not on those pages; the following are examples, not an exhaustive count: at line 109815-109816 the sanctoral gives '31 May - Feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Queen / Page 1298g', and at lines 197554-197568 the general index carries an 'Appendix' block naming the Queenship, St Isidore the Farmer, St Frances Xavier Cabrini and St Pius X. These references are post-1954 insertions into the body of this printing, so the recorded exclusions by page range are not a complete account of the printing's new matter. They are retained because they are feast titles and page numbers -- pointers, not the excluded pages' expression -- and because deleting body text the exclusions do not name would put an undisclosed editorial hand into the bytes. A reader must not take them as dating evidence and must not reconstruct the appendix from them. Printed p. 1302d begins the following Common of a Martyr-Bishop before the page break, so retained ordinary p. 1303 necessarily opens mid-prayer; that incompleteness is deliberate because restoring the missing opening would reintroduce expression from the excluded leaf.

OCR QUALITY. Measured here by scripts/_ocr_quality.py at a function-word share of en=0.2444 and la=0.0827 over 695,938 tokens, classified prose-english. The two figures must be read together and against a monolingual comparator: the book prints Latin and English in facing columns, so neither language can approach the 0.39-0.41 a keyed English text reaches, and their sum of 0.33 is the number that means the pages are prose. Individual lines are nonetheless corrupt in the ordinary ways -- 'Benriger' for Benziger at line 70, 'Missat' for Missal, running heads fused to body text -- and diacritics on the Latin survive unevenly. Quote from this artifact only through a checked passage, and do not rest a negative search on it: the raw-line modes establish absence of a string, not absence of a text.

IDENTITY. A printing of about 1955-56 of the 1945 revised edition, not the 1937 first edition; see the edition record. The literal 'http://ccwatershed.org' page-foot stamp survives 1,845 times and is the scan host's watermark, carrying no notice and no claim.

The New Roman Missal was registered twice and neither registration was renewed in its twenty-eighth year: A 110108, copyright 15 July 1937, renewal window closed 15 July 1965; A 192159, copyright 1 November 1945, renewal window closed 1 November 1973. The finding was made at registration-number level across five bodies of the Copyright Office's published record and carries three positive controls drawn from the same OCR layer, so that the negative could be distinguished from a failed search; it is recorded in full, with its citations, its caveats and what would overturn it, at src/sources/inventories/lasance-new-roman-missal-rights-v1.toml. The 'Copyright, 1936, by Benziger Brothers' notice printed in the book is not disturbed and does not need to be: a notice establishes that a term began, and that record establishes that it ended. THE LETTERED INSERTS AT PRINTED PAGES 1298a-1298n AND 1302a-1302d ARE NOT COVERED BY THAT BASIS AND ARE NOT IN THESE BYTES. They contain new matter not established as part of either unrenewed registration, and both page-bounded ranges were removed by the transformation named below rather than carried across and disclaimed in prose. Supp. 2d 191 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)), and machine optical character recognition adds no human authorship on top of it: this text layer was produced autonomously by tesseract 5.3.0, and there is no author to hold a right in it. That is the same reasoning this repository already applies to the CMAA facsimile at guidance/missals.md:325-346, with the difference that there it stood alone and disposed only of a licence, while here the underlying work has an affirmative basis of its own and the scan argument completes the case instead of substituting for one. work.author: Francis Xavier Lasance and Francis Augustine Walsh
work.description: A commercial hand missal compiled by Francis Xavier Lasance (1860-1946) and Francis Augustine Walsh, O.S.B. (1884-1938), published by Benziger Brothers and printed with the Latin of the Missale Romanum facing an English rendering, together with the compilers' own prefaces, instructions, meditations, saints' lives, glossary of liturgical terms and prayers for private devotion, and William R. Kelly's illustrated study plan 'Read Mass with the Priest'. It is a devotional book made for a layperson following the Mass, not an official liturgical book and not an approved English edition of any typical edition: its English is its compilers' and carries no authority of its own. It witnesses what an English-speaking Catholic of the mid twentieth century read alongside the altar book, and any use of it as evidence for the Roman Rite must say so. The work is named for its compilers rather than for the Church because the compilation, the arrangement and the English are theirs; the Latin it prints belongs to work.catholic-church.missale-romanum and is not made this work's by being reprinted here.
